title: The bond market isn’t panicking – it’s repricing for a riskier world
gist: Thirty-year yields in several major economies have touched their highest levels since 2007, but the move is driven almost entirely by rising term premia — compensation for fiscal, inflation and geopolitical risk — rather than by expectations of higher policy rates (Japan being the exception, where the whole curve is repricing higher policy rates). The core argument is regime-change, not crisis: the ultra-low term premia of the GFC-to-COVID era were an anomaly created by weak growth, disinflation and QE, and even if yields retrace, they will not return to those levels; the danger to watch is a disorderly, forced-selling episode of the 2022 UK gilt type, and the only real fix is fiscal consolidation in the US, France and the UK.

insights.claim: Yields on thirty-year government bonds have touched their highest levels since 2007 in several major economies, yet this is explicitly characterised as not yet a bond market crisis.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Anchors the move as a regime repricing rather than a dislocation — argues against buying duration on the assumption of a snap-back, but also against positioning for imminent systemic stress.
insights.quote: This is not yet a bond market crisis.

insights.claim: The largest increases in bond yields have occurred in the economies with the greatest fiscal risks — the US, UK, France and Italy — and the rise has been concentrated at the long end of the curve, with shorter-dated yields rising by less.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Fiscal risk, not policy-rate expectations, is the sorting variable across sovereigns — favours curve steepeners and relative-value shorts in high-deficit issuers over outright duration views.

insights.claim: Japan is the exception to the global pattern: its government bond yields are rising across the whole curve because markets are pricing higher policy rates, rather than demanding more compensation for long-duration risk.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: JGBs are a different trade from Treasuries, gilts and OATs — a policy-rate story that supports the yen and front-end shorts, not a term-premium/fiscal story.

insights.claim: Most of the recent increase in bond yields has been driven by term premia — the additional compensation investors demand for holding bonds — rather than by expectations for short-term interest rates over time.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Decomposing yields into rate expectations versus term premium is the analytical key: rate cuts alone will not repair the long end if the premium component is doing the work.
insights.locator: The yields of bonds reflect expectations

insights.claim: There has been no obvious economic or market trigger for the latest bond sell-off: energy prices rose but nowhere near as sharply as during the earlier stages of the Iran conflict, fiscal positions are strained but did not suddenly deteriorate, and changes in the investor base are gradual.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: A trigger-less sell-off implies slow-burn structural repricing rather than an event that can be faded — reduces the case for mean-reversion trades keyed to a specific catalyst reversing.
insights.quote: It is striking that there has been no obvious economic or market trigger for the latest bond sell-off.
insights.locator: A permanent shift

themes.theme: Drivers of the term-premium regime shift

insights.claim: Fiscal positions have deteriorated materially across much of the developed world, with high debt, large deficits and little political appetite for the consolidation needed to put public finances on a clearly sustainable path — with Japan again the exception.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Persistent supply plus absent political will means the fiscal risk premium is structural, keeping long-end sovereigns as a chronic source of volatility rather than a safe carry asset.
insights.locator: There are several reasons for this.

insights.claim: Geopolitical shocks such as the Iran war are inherently stagflationary, which makes them uniquely damaging for long-dated nominal bonds because they raise inflation risk and growth risk simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Stagflationary shocks break the equity-bond hedge, so duration is a poorer portfolio diversifier in this regime; argues for inflation-linked exposure and commodity hedges instead.
insights.quote: the world is more prone to geopolitical shocks, and that these shocks are inherently stagflationary
insights.locator: The inflation environment is also more uncertain

insights.claim: The more important source of monetary-policy uncertainty is not new Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's push to reduce forward guidance, but that his muddled communications have left markets less certain about the Fed's policy framework itself.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Framework ambiguity at the Fed is a persistent term-premium and rate-vol tax — supports owning optionality (long rate vol) and discounting Fed communication as a source of duration comfort.
insights.quote: the bigger issue is that his muddled communications have left markets less certain about the Fed’s policy framework
insights.locator: And uncertainty around monetary policy has increased.

insights.claim: The exceptionally low term premia between the Global Financial Crisis and the COVID pandemic were the product of an unusual combination of weak growth, persistent disinflationary pressures and extraordinarily accommodative policy including large-scale central-bank bond purchases — an anomaly, not a baseline.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Any valuation model anchored to 2009-2019 term premia is mis-specified; long-run discount rates, pension liability assumptions and equity risk premia all need re-basing higher.
insights.locator: However, even if yields fall back

insights.claim: Part of the rise in yields is a return to economic normality rather than a pathology: deflation is no longer the biggest threat, unemployment has fallen, and central-bank balance sheets have shrunk.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Reframes higher long yields as a normalisation to be underwritten rather than a crisis to be hedged — tempers doom-narrative positioning while still ruling out a return to prior lows.
insights.locator: In some ways this reflects a return to economic normality

insights.claim: Pension funds and insurers have become less important marginal buyers of long-duration government debt at the same time that governments are issuing substantially more of it, so it would be surprising if investors accepted the same historically low term premia as before.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: A demand-side structural shift, not just supply: the price-insensitive long-end bid has weakened, so ultra-long auctions and issuance calendars become tradeable risk events.
insights.locator: But governments are issuing substantially more debt

themes.theme: Why the macro damage is contained — so far

insights.claim: The sell-off has been concentrated at the very long end of yield curves, which has relatively little influence on household and corporate borrowing costs; ten-year yields matter considerably more for transmission to the real economy.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Watch the 10-year, not the 30-year, as the trigger level for real-economy damage — headlines about 30-year record yields overstate the immediate macro hit.
insights.locator: Economic consequences are manageable – so far

insights.claim: Corporate bond spreads remain tight and bond-market volatility has risen but not to the levels seen during the major dislocations of 2022 and 2023, indicating no broad tightening in financial conditions yet.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Credit spreads and option-implied Treasury vol are the two live dashboards; a breakout in either toward 2022-23 levels is the signal that the bond adjustment has become a macro shock.
insights.locator: Corporate bond spreads remain tight

insights.claim: The specific danger is that the repricing turns disorderly, generating losses for leveraged investors and forcing them to sell into a falling market — the same dynamic that drove the 2022 UK gilt crisis.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: The tail risk is a leverage-unwind, not a slow yield grind; monitor leveraged basis and liability-driven positioning as the accelerant that converts repricing into a financial-conditions shock.
insights.quote: The danger is that the repricing becomes disorderly, generating losses for leveraged investors and forcing them to sell assets into a falling market.
insights.locator: The danger is that the repricing becomes disorderly

insights.claim: Rising yields should not automatically be treated as a policy problem, because to some extent the market is doing exactly what it is supposed to do — pricing risk.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Lowers the odds of pre-emptive official support at current levels, so investors should not expect a policy put to cap long-end yields.
insights.locator: A fiscal problem

insights.claim: Central banks should intervene only when a rapid sell-off threatens financial stability — as the Bank of England did in 2022 by temporarily buying long-dated gilts to stop a forced-selling spiral — and should not suppress yields that are rising because investors demand compensation for fiscal and inflation risks.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Gives a testable rule for when official bids appear: financial-stability stress, not yield levels — so fading long-end sell-offs on hopes of central-bank buying is a poor trade absent forced selling.
insights.quote: If yields are rising because investors are demanding more compensation for fiscal and inflation risks, central banks should not try to suppress the move.
insights.locator: Central banks will only become concerned

themes.theme: Debt management is not fiscal consolidation

insights.claim: Governments are easing long-end pressure through issuance composition rather than fiscal action: Japan has reduced the supply of very long-dated bonds and the US has increased its reliance on Treasury bills.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Shortening the weighted-average maturity shifts risk from the long end to rollover/front-end exposure — bullish for bills demand and a structural steepening bias, with the debt burden more sensitive to future policy rates.
insights.locator: Governments can ease pressure at the margin

insights.claim: The US Treasury's announcement that it will double the size of its buyback operations at the 10 to 30-year part of the curve is a signalling device whose sums are small, and it delivered only temporary reprieve to the bond market.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Treats the buyback expansion as a fade rather than a durable support — a template for reading future technical announcements as short-lived rallies to sell.
insights.quote: These moves send a signal to markets, but the sums involved are small.
insights.locator: The announcement last week that the US Treasury

insights.claim: The largest fiscal adjustments are required in the US, France and the UK, and given limited political appetite for consolidation — particularly in the US — bond markets are likely to remain vulnerable to further bouts of volatility.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Names the three sovereigns where recurring long-end stress is most likely — a watchlist for volatility trades, curve steepeners and sovereign relative-value across USTs, OATs and gilts.
insights.locator: Governments with unsustainable fiscal trajectories

insights.claim: Some of the recent rise in yields may unwind, but upward pressure on term premia is expected to be a lasting feature of the post-pandemic age because debt burdens are higher, inflation risks less predictable and political willingness to fix fiscal problems limited.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: The structural call: treat retracements as tactical, not a return to the old regime — long-run asset allocation should assume a permanently higher risk-free discount rate.
insights.quote: But the old world is gone, and these underlying forces mean upward pressure on term premia is likely to be a lasting feature of the post-pandemic age.
insights.locator: The bond market is therefore sending a rational message

insights.claim: A crackdown on illegal Chinese exports — what the White House calls the 'Great Transhipment Scam' — would have only a small impact on trade flows in aggregate, according to accompanying data and analysis.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Argues against pricing large trade-flow disruption into Asian exporter or logistics names on transhipment-enforcement headlines.
insights.locator: In case you missed it

insights.claim: Collapsing exports of internal-combustion-engine models have pushed the euro-zone's trade balance in cars into a deep deficit, pointing to further declines in European auto production ahead.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: A structural short signal for European auto OEMs and their supplier chains, and a drag on euro-zone industrial output and the current account.
insights.locator: Collapsing exports of models with internal combustion engines
